summary: Defines a PANA extension for establishing a security association in advance between a client in one access network and an authentication agent in another network it may move to. It is an experimental specification.

eli5.summary: You sign in at the next building before leaving the current one, so you walk right in.

questions: authenticate before moving to a new network
subtitle: Authenticate with a future network before switching to it.

tldr.problem: Mobile devices that move between networks must re-authenticate each time, creating a handover delay that disrupts applications. When a device switches networks, it must wait for the authentication process to complete before it can use the network.
tldr.mechanism: PANA pre-authentication allows a mobile client to conduct authentication with a Candidate Authentication Agent in another access network before arriving there. The client proactively establishes a security association with the future network using an extended PANA header with a pre-authentication bit, so authentication completes before or during handover.
tldr.outcome: The device can attach to the new network immediately upon arrival without waiting for full authentication. This enables seamless handover for mobile applications that cannot tolerate connection disruption.

today: RFC 5873 is Experimental. Pre-authentication remains a specialized technique for reducing handover latency in mobile networks. Adoption has been limited, and the specification has not advanced to Standards Track.

sections.title: What is PANA Pre-Authentication
sections.content:
PANA (Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access) is a protocol that carries EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) messages between a client and an authentication agent in an access network. The RFC extends PANA to support pre-authentication: a PANA Client can start authentication with a Candidate Authentication Agent in another network before physically moving there.

When a mobile device is in one access network but can see other potential networks nearby, it can use pre-authentication to negotiate security credentials with the new network in advance. Once the device moves and connects to that network, authentication is already complete, eliminating handover latency.
sections.eli5: You contact the security office at the next building and show your badge while you are still in the current one. When you walk over, they already know who you are.

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.content:
The RFC introduces several terms for this process. The Serving Network is the access network the client is currently attached to. The Candidate Network is a potential target network for future handover. The Serving PAA (Serving PANA Authentication Agent) is the current authenticator, and the Candidate PAA (Candidate PANA Authentication Agent) is the future authenticator in the target network.

The pre-authentication process uses the same EAP exchange as normal authentication but with an extra marker in the PANA header. The device may conduct pre-authentication with multiple networks at once to prepare for a choice of where to move.
sections.eli5: You have a PAA at your current building and a PAA at the next building. Pre-authentication means you talk to the next building's PAA while still in the current one.

sections.title: The Pre-Authentication Procedure
sections.content:
Pre-authentication is initiated by the client sending a PANA-Client-Initiation (PCI) message with a new 'E' (pre-authentication) bit set. The Candidate PAA responds with a PANA-Auth-Request (PAR) message, also with the 'E' bit set, indicating that it supports and accepts pre-authentication.

Once both sides agree to pre-authenticate, all subsequent messages between the client and the Candidate PAA carry the 'E' bit set. The client and PAA complete the full EAP authentication exchange. A PANA Security Association is established and stored on the client and PAA, but not yet activated for the data path.

When the client actually moves to the new network and detects the switch, it sends a Notification message with the 'E' bit cleared. At this point, the Candidate PAA becomes the Serving PAA and the pre-established security association takes effect immediately. The client can begin using the network without re-authenticating.
sections.eli5: Step 1: You send a message saying 'I want to pre-authenticate.' Step 2: The next building says 'OK, go ahead.' Step 3: You do the full sign-in process while still in the current building. Step 4: When you walk to the new building, you just notify them you are here, and you are logged in.

sections.title: PANA Header Extension
sections.content:
The PANA message header uses a Flags field with bits to indicate different message properties. The RFC allocates bit 6 of this field as the new 'E' (pre-authentication) bit. When set to 1, this bit indicates that the PANA message is part of a pre-authentication exchange.

The 'E' bit is set in both PCI messages from the client and PAR messages from the Candidate PAA when they agree to pre-authenticate. It remains set in all messages of the pre-authentication exchange until the client actually moves and sends a notification message clearing the bit.
sections.eli5: A single bit in the PANA message header acts as a flag saying 'this is pre-authentication, not regular authentication.' Both sides check this bit to know what mode they are in.

sections.title: Compatibility with Existing PANA Implementations
sections.content:
When a client sends a PCI message with the 'E' bit set to a PAA that does not support pre-authentication, the PAA ignores the unfamiliar bit and treats it as a normal authentication attempt. The PAA responds with a PAR message without the 'E' bit set.

The client detects this mismatch and terminates the connection, as per the RFC. This ensures that pre-authentication is only used when both sides support it. The mechanism has been designed so that adding support for pre-authentication does not break existing PANA deployments.
sections.eli5: If the new building's office does not understand your pre-authentication request, they ignore it and treat it as a normal sign-in. You notice the mismatch and try something else. Nothing breaks.

sections.title: Security and Denial-of-Service Protection
sections.content:
Pre-authentication creates a potential security risk: an attacker can send PCI messages from anywhere on the Internet, not just from physically adjacent networks, and force a PAA to create state for every attack message. This could be a denial-of-service vector.

The RFC recommends that PAAs follow PANA best practices to stay stateless when possible (as described in RFC 5191). Additionally, it suggests that PAAs should only accept pre-authentication messages from clients on known, well-trusted networks. For example, a PAA could whitelist certain IP ranges or ASNs from which pre-authentication is permitted. This geolocation-based filtering can prevent attacks from distant networks while still allowing legitimate handover scenarios.
sections.eli5: A bad person could pretend to be in the next building and trick it into setting up lots of fake authentication sessions. So the building should only accept pre-authentication requests from people who are visibly in certain nearby networks.
